analysis.one_liner: Sets federal standards for health plans, bans lifetime coverage caps and health-based premium discrimination, and guarantees patients choice of plan type and appeal rights.
analysis.headline: The health insurance consumer protections in the bill never advanced past the Senate committee they were referred to, with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set federal rules for all health plans, including self-insured ones. It banned lifetime benefit limits, barred insurers from setting premiums or denying coverage based on health status or genetic risk, and sharply limited pre-existing-condition exclusions. It required employers to offer workers a choice among a managed care plan, a point-of-service plan, and a traditional fee-for-service plan, and it required plans to cover emergency room visits without pre-authorization, run appeal processes with independent review, disclose their financial incentives in plain language, and maintain enough providers — including specialists — to actually serve enrollees. The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, people with pre-existing conditions, chronic illnesses, and genetic risk would have gained guaranteed, renewable coverage without health-status premiums or lifetime caps. Workers with employer coverage would have gained a guaranteed choice of plan type, including a fee-for-service option. All enrollees would have gained stronger appeal rights, emergency coverage without pre-authorization, plain-language disclosure of what plans restrict, and protection against insurers using financial incentives to deny care. Small employers and individuals buying through associations would have gained the same protections, plus consumer counseling offices in every state.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and people with health conditions

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits lifetime benefit limits, so a catastrophic illness could no longer exhaust someone's coverage (Sec. 505).
Bars setting premiums or limiting coverage based on health status, medical history, disability, or genetic predisposition, and requires guaranteed issue and renewal of coverage (Secs. 501-502).
Requires plans to cover emergency room care whenever symptoms reasonably suggest an emergency, without preauthorization and regardless of whether the hospital is in-network (Sec. 303(e)).
Bans financial incentives that pay reviewers to deny medically necessary care and requires a physician to review any denial of coverage (Sec. 303(c)).

Requires plans to maintain adequate provider networks, including specialists and rural access, to disclose their terms and financial incentives in plain language, to run real grievance and appeals processes, and to protect patient record confidentiality (Title IV).
Gives every employee a choice among a managed care plan, a point-of-service plan, and a traditional fee-for-service plan, and funds a consumer counseling office in each state (Titles I-II).

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans would have borne the cost: they could no longer underwrite, market, or deny care the way the bill restricted, and would face certification, solvency, disclosure, and review requirements. Employers would have faced a mandate to offer at least three plan types, including a fee-for-service option many had dropped. Some costs would likely have flowed to premiums.

drawbacks.text: Every employer offering health coverage would have had to offer and administer at least three plan types — managed care, point-of-service, and traditional fee-for-service — which smaller employers said would add administrative complexity and cost.

The bill barred plans from using financial incentives to limit care and required physician review of denials, which insurers argued would raise premiums; critics of the era also warned that guaranteed issue without a strong individual mandate can push healthy people out of the pool and raise prices for everyone else, though the bill's risk-adjustment program (Sec. 504) was designed partly to counter that.

The bill still allowed up to six months of pre-existing-condition exclusion and age-rating premiums up to 2-to-1 between youngest and oldest adults, so it would not have eliminated all out-of-pocket barriers for sick or older enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have been large for patients with pre-existing conditions, chronic illness, or limited plan choices, and for patients subject to arbitrary coverage denials. The costs were real but moderate: insurers and managed care plans would have faced new certification, solvency, disclosure, and review requirements that raise administrative costs, and employers would have had to offer a fee-for-service option they had largely dropped. An honest assessment is that the bill traded higher administrative costs and reduced insurer flexibility for far stronger protections against the practices that most harmed patients — lifetime caps, health-status underwriting, and unreviewed denial of necessary care. It was never seriously debated, so its design was never stress-tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 23, 1995 by Senator Wellstone.
On the same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; the Congressional record shows no committee markup, floor vote, or movement after the referral.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care companies, which avoided the new standards and continued the practices the bill would have restricted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, untouched by the rules

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke on the Senate floor upon introduction, then saw it referred to committee with no follow-up action.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in March 1995 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no cosponsors in a Republican-controlled Senate, and its single liberal Democratic sponsor was unable to move it past the committee stage.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill imposed federal certification, solvency, disclosure, network-adequacy, and utilization-review requirements on all plans, and banned health-status underwriting and lifetime caps. Plans' business practices of cherry-picking healthy enrollees and limiting care to control costs would have been sharply constrained. Sources: [S2], [S3].

For the first time, self-insured plans (currently exempt from most state insurance regulation under ERISA) would have faced federal solvency and plan standards enforceable by the Labor Department. This closed a major regulatory gap but added compliance costs. Sources: [S2], [S3].

The bill required objective, transparent credentialing, due process before termination from plan networks, and a ban on discriminating against professionals based on license type or their patients' health needs — protections providers sought against plan gatekeeping. Sources: [S2], [S3].

States could certify plans as meeting federal utilization-review standards based on accreditation by a nationally recognized nonprofit accreditation entity, routing regulatory reliance through bodies like the NCQA. Sources: [S2], [S3].
